Q. 118. Why is the charge of keeping the sabbath more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors?

A. The charge of keeping the sabbath is more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors, because they are bound not only to keep it themselves, but to see that it be observed by all those that are under their charge; and because they are prone ofttimes to hinder them by employments of their own.

relationships.title: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery

occurrences.excerpt: …Session minutes be cited for an exception of substance based on WLC 117, WLC 118, WCF 21:8, and BCO 40-2. After floor debate, the RSR Committee motion failed. A subsequent motion to approve the Redeemer Church minutes without exception carried.

metadata.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

relationships.title: Wilson et al. v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

occurrences.excerpt: …residing under the unique, but constitutional, guardianship of their parents (WLC 118, 124; BCO 28-1; 28-5).

metadata.synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.
